This is a highly distinctive, mechanistically informative presentation: unilateral, sole-specific tingling-pain *exclusively triggered by leg elevation above chest level*, resolving rapidly with dependency. The absence of motor deficit, systemic symptoms, or left-sided involvement rules out central, radicular, and bilateral neuropathic processes. Critically, the symptom is *not provoked by activity, posture in neutral position, or nerve compression maneuvers* — making classic entrapment (e.g., tarsal tunnel) or radiculopathy implausible. Instead, it is exquisitely tied to a hemodynamic challenge: elevation reduces hydrostatic pressure in the distal microvasculature. In a patient with dual endothelial insults — long-standing T2DM (HbA1c 7.2%) and extreme smoking burden (68 pack-years) — this creates a “perfusion reserve failure” scenario. The sole of the foot is uniquely vulnerable: high metabolic demand, sparse collateral supply, and dependence on distal capillary perfusion pressure. The rapid resolution upon dependency confirms reversibility — consistent with transient ischemia, not structural nerve injury or infarction. All other alternatives (SFN, radiculopathy, venous congestion, medication effect) fail to explain the strict positional trigger, unilateral sole localization, and immediate reversibility. No lab, imaging, or exam finding contradicts this; pending tests (duplex, NCS, monofilament) are appropriately aimed at *ruling out mimics*, not confirming the diagnosis — which is already strongly supported by pattern recognition.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Symptom is strictly localized to the sole of the right foot.  
- Symptom occurs *only* when leg is elevated above chest level.  
- Symptom fully resolves within minutes of returning to dependent position.  
- No motor deficit (no foot drop, no gait instability).  
- No systemic red flags (no fever, weight loss, bowel/bladder dysfunction, autonomic symptoms).  
- No left-foot involvement — strictly unilateral.  
- Patient has 34-year, 2-pack-per-day smoking history (68 pack-years).  
- Patient has 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus with suboptimal glycemic control (HbA1c 7.2%).  
- Exercise-induced calf cramps on incline suggest underlying ischemic susceptibility.  
- Symptom is *not* provoked by standing, walking, sitting, coughing, Valsalva, or neutral-posture movement — only by elevation.  

[GAPS]  
- Absence of direct microvascular perfusion assessment (e.g., laser Doppler flowmetry during elevation, toe-brachial index).  
- No tibial nerve conduction study or medial plantar sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) results reported yet — though ordered, their outcome would help exclude subtle focal neuropathy.  
- No skin temperature or color assessment of the affected sole during symptom provocation (e.g., pallor/cyanosis on elevation).  
- No documentation of capillary refill time or dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulse quality *during symptom onset* (i.e., while elevated).  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Positional Plantar Paresthesia Secondary to Diabetic-Smoking Microangiopathy

[THOUGHT]  
This is a highly distinctive, mechanistically informative presentation: unilateral, sole-specific tingling-pain *exclusively triggered by leg elevation above chest level*, resolving rapidly with dependency. The absence of motor deficit, systemic symptoms, or left-sided involvement rules out central, radicular, and bilateral neuropathic processes. Critically, the symptom is *not provoked by activity, posture in neutral position, or nerve compression maneuvers* — making classic entrapment (e.g., tarsal tunnel) or radiculopathy implausible. Instead, it is exquisitely tied to a hemodynamic challenge: elevation reduces hydrostatic pressure in the distal microvasculature. In a patient with dual endothelial insults — long-standing T2DM (HbA1c 7.2%) and extreme smoking burden (68 pack-years) — this creates a “perfusion reserve failure” scenario. The sole of the foot is uniquely vulnerable: high metabolic demand, sparse collateral supply, and dependence on distal capillary perfusion pressure. The rapid resolution upon dependency confirms reversibility — consistent with transient ischemia, not structural nerve injury or infarction. All other alternatives (SFN, radiculopathy, venous congestion, medication effect) fail to explain the strict positional trigger, unilateral sole localization, and immediate reversibility. No lab, imaging, or exam finding contradicts this; pending tests (duplex, NCS, monofilament) are appropriately aimed at *ruling out mimics*, not confirming the diagnosis — which is already strongly supported by pattern recognition.
